'''Betty Wright Harris''' (born July 29, 1940) is an American [[chemist]]. She is known for her work on the chemistry of explosives completed at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]]. She patented a spot test for detecting 1,3,5-triamino-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene ([[TATB]]) in the field,  which is used by the Federal Department of Homeland Security to screen for nitroaromatic explosives.<ref name="Alumnae in Science, Technology, and Health">{{cite web|title=Alumnae in Science, Technology, and Health|url=https://www.cau.edu/news/womens-history-month.html|publisher=Clark Atlanta University|accessdate=2020-06-10}}</ref><ref name=sciencemakers>{{cite book|title=The HistoryMakers ScienceMaker Toolkit|publisher=thehistorymakers.com|url=http://www.thehistorymakers.com/sites/production/files/Toolkit%20Vol%202-3.pdf|accessdate=2014-07-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160819052406/http://www.thehistorymakers.com/sites/production/files/Toolkit%20Vol%202-3.pdf|archive-date=19 August 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Harris was born on 29 July 1940<ref name="Intro Necessary">{{cite web|title=Betty Harris|url=https://introductionsnecessary.com/podcast/betty-harris/|website=Introductions Necessary|publisher=Nine Hour Films|accessdate=23 March 2017|date=29 July 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190423201514/https://introductionsnecessary.com/podcast/betty-harris/|archive-date=23 April 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref> in [[Ouachita Parish, Louisiana|Ouachita Parish]], [[Monroe, Louisiana]]. She and her 11 siblings were raised on a farm by Henry Hudson "Jake" and Legertha Evelyn Thompson Wright.<ref name="CPNAS Betty Harris">{{cite web|title=Betty W. Harris|url=http://www.cpnas.org/aahp/biographies/betty-w-harris.html|publisher=National Academies of Science|accessdate=2014-07-12|archive-date=17 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190817133849/http://www.cpnas.org/aahp/biographies/betty-w-harris.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> She attended Union Central High School, enrolling at [[Southern University]] at the age of 16. She received her B.S. in chemistry with a minor in mathematics at the age of 19 and subsequently attended [[Atlanta University]], receiving her M.S. degree.<ref name="Betty Wright Harris">{{cite web|last1=Mahoney|first1=Eleanor|title=BETTY WRIGHT HARRIS (1940-)|date=27 January 2018 |url=https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/harris-betty-wright-1940/|accessdate=2020-06-10}}</ref><ref name="IBTBetty Harris">{{cite news|last1=Osborne|first1=Hannah|title=Black History Month 2014 Five Black Chemists who Changed the World Honoured|url=https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/black-history-month-2014-five-black-chemists-who-changed-world-honoured-1435102|accessdate=2014-07-12|work=International Business Times}}</ref> She taught as an assistant professor of chemistry and mathematics<ref name=MWBettyHarris>{{cite web|last1=Woodlief|first1=Mayona|title=Biography of Dr. Betty Harris|url=https://mayonawoodlief.wordpress.com/2013/04/29/biography-of-dr-betty-harris/|date=2013-04-29 |accessdate=2014-07-12}}</ref> at [[Mississippi Valley State University]], [[Southern University]] and [[Colorado College]].<ref name=sciencemakers />

Harris was awarded a PhD in chemistry from the University of New Mexico in 1975, with a dissertation titled "Reactions of 2-aminopyridine with picryl halides".<ref name="Harris PhD">{{cite book|last1=Harris|first1=Betsy Wright|title=Reactions of 2-aminopyridine with picryl halides|date=1975|publisher=University of New Mexico|url=https://unm.on.worldcat.org/oclc/2506840|accessdate=23 March 2017}}</ref>

==Career==

After gaining her PhD, she taught chemistry and mathematics at [[Mississippi Valley State University]] and [[Southern University]].<ref name="Betty Wright Harris"/> Harris subsequently moved to do research at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], where she worked in the areas of [[hazardous waste treatment]] and [[environmental remediation]] as well as explosives chemistry. Areas of focus included explosives detection, safing liquids, synthesis and characterization of insensitive high explosives and sensitivity of weathered high explosives.<ref name=blackinventionsbettyharris>{{cite web|title=Featured Inventors: Dr. Betty Harris|url=http://blackinventions.org/featuredinventors.htm|publisher=International Black Inventions Museum|accessdate=2014-07-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140311041428/http://blackinventions.org/featuredinventors.htm|archive-date=11 March 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> In addition to her research, she has worked in outreach to young people, including working with the Girl Scouts in developing a badge based on chemistry.

During a leave of absence from LANL, Harris was the chief of chemical technology for Solar Turbine Inc., where she managed the technical laboratories and investigated cold-end corrosion of super alloys, which was caused by [[sulfuric acid]] and soot in gas turbine engines. For the last eleven years of Harris's career, she worked at the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Classification as a certified document reviewer.<ref name="CPNAS Betty Harris" />

==Awards==

She has received the New Mexico Governor's Trailblazer Award,<ref name=black-inventorbettyharris>{{cite web|title=Dr. Betty Harris|url=http://www.black-inventor.com/Dr-Betty-Harris.asp|publisher=Famous Black Inventions|accessdate=2014-07-12}}</ref> and is recognized as a distinguished African American Scientist by the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="CPNAS Betty Harris" /> She is a member of [[Women in Science and Engineering]] and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and served as President of the [[New Mexico Business and Professional Women's Organization]].<ref name="Betty Wright Harris"/> She is a 50-year member of the [[American Chemical Society]].

==Personal life==
Harris lives in Los Alamos, NM and has three children.<ref name=sciencemakers />
